data.title: CUPE 5089 condemn moves by Toronto Police Services to expand in TTC and take over members’ work
data.description:
CUPE 5089 condemn moves by Toronto Police Services to expand in TTC and take over members’ work

Union argues growth of TPS presence in transit system won’t address core safety issues

Toronto Police Services representatives have indicated they intend to take over major roles in station security on the TTC, per conversations between CUPE 5089 President Denver Sanmuganthan and TPS.

“This is a serious encroachment into our members’ work and will not help keep riders safe” said Sanmuganthan. “When the police show up to our stations, our Special Constables have to direct them every step of the way. They do not know the system with any level of detail, unlike our members.”

Five stations have already been identified as initial priorities for TPS: Eglinton Station, Finch Station, Kennedy Station, Kipling Station, and Union Station. TPS will additionally add between 4 and 12 officers to Line 1 and 2. They have already indicated plans to expand significantly, partially dependent on the new municipal councillors and the recently re-elected Mayor Chow.

CUPE 5089 members are key in maintaining a safe and secure TTC system in Toronto. They are trained in public safety, health, emergency and deescalation techniques. There are no additional powers that police can exercise in the TTC. The only difference between TPS officers and Special Constables is that police are equipped with firearms and other tools.

Crucially, Special Constables are very familiar with the TTC system itself, including the layout and architecture of stations, including tunnels, blind spots, and odd corners. As frontline safety workers, they are at higher risk of assault. Indeed, assaults against workers and patrons has gone up since the pandemic, despite overall crime declining in this period by almost every measure.

TPS made similar indications that they wanted to expand into TTC stations in 2016. Upon receiving a funding increase for that initiative, TPS instead created new patrol positions outside the TTC.

When the old Transit Patrol Unit of the TPS was disbanded, TPS said the unit was “no longer required” because the TTC had “a highly capable Special Constable Program”.

Since 2016 there have been resources committed to safety on the TTC, including a 10-point action plan to prevent assaults on workers in 2022, and $4.9 million in the 2023 budget to go towards 10 new Streets to Homes outreach workers, 25 Special Constables, and a one-year pilot project with the mental health team M-DOT.

It should be noted that these reforms were not aimed to address criminal incidents. A report authored by the TTC itself states that “there is no empirical evidence that persons experiencing homelessness and individuals with complex needs are related to increased safety incidents on the TTC.”

The union argues that funding for Special Constables as well as promotion of initiatives like Streets to Homes is more effective than adding police officers to the TTC.

CUPE 5089 is circulating a Change.org petition to garner public opposition to this move by TPS and instead strengthen the Special Constables program, which you can access at this link.

data.title: Clearing out my parents' house was a legal nightmare. How can I downsize without putting my kids through the same ordeal?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

Some countercultural advice this Black Friday: stop buying stuff, plus other rules for downsizing

"Legal fees ended up eating up half the value of my parents' estate." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I have recently read and heard a lot about the recommendation for seniors to take an active role in managing their estates - specifically by downsizing, in addition to having the wills and estate plans you have advised for years. Downsizing means going through all the "stuff" accumulated over the years and weeding out the treasures and clutter we no longer use, need or want.

While many seniors do this when they move into a retirement community, plenty of us stay put in our homes for decades. My parents lived in their home from 1950 to 2020. They believed their children would enjoy going through their belongings and reminiscing after they passed, but the reality was quite different and a massive hassle.

None of us lived nearby, we argued over what to do with 70 years' worth of possessions, and eventually, lawyers and the courts got involved. Legal fees ate up half the value of my parents' estate. Downsizing is difficult because of sentimental attachments, the sheer physical energy it requires and the challenge of knowing what is valuable versus what to let go of.

In my own downsizing efforts, I've avoided the hassle of online listings, garage sales or hiring estate experts, opting instead to give things to neighbors, donate them to Goodwill or toss them. What advice can you share for seniors who have too much stuff, feel overwhelmed by the process and want to spare their families what mine went through?

Aging Downsizer

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My husband wants to sell our $1.5 million home and downsize. But this is where we raised our kids - and I can't bear to leave.

You will be surprised how quickly you forget about items once they're gone.

Dear Downsizer,

Sticky notes on furniture is no substitute for a proper will.

Your experience clearing out your parents' home is a cautionary tale. Hiring lawyers can cost a fortune and escalate disagreements that could be better resolved with a mediator. When it comes to family, going to court should be the very last resort. Aging parents can start giving away their valuable items to their children in an effort to prevent arguments later on, or put in place a system for choosing them, such as labeling items or drawing straws and allowing each child to choose an item in rotation.

Be aware that giving away expensive antiques, jewelry, or furniture during your lifetime with a combined value exceeding $19,000 per recipient in a single calendar year will require you to file a gift-tax return (IRS Form 709), even though you won't actually owe taxes unless you exceed the multi-million-dollar lifetime exemption. An important sticky note for your estate plans: Naming a third party as executor, and giving them authority in your will to sell any items your children can't agree upon within, say, 30 days, will help keep any family disputes out of court.

Without further ado - and I hope this helps you - here are some tips for clearing your house:

5 rules of downsizing

(1) Be tough. Without throwing out something valuable like an antique, a letter from a loved one or a wedding photo album that can never be replaced, you have to be ruthless when downsizing. And while the struggle is real, you need to avoid engaging in it every time you open a box. Your memories are not packed away in an attic or basement. They are in your mind and they are in your heart.

(2) Think digital. After you have had the hard conversations with your children about what they want or what they don't want, you can take photos of a treasured childhood toy before donating it or throwing it in the garbage. And a Kindle or the Apple Books app takes up less space than thousands of physical books.You can always put your favorite memories on social media or put them in a shared online folder so family members have access to them.

(3) Take it easy. The emotional labor is as challenging as the physical labor. You are, after all, sifting through your memories, which will bring up good and possibly also bad or painful moments. Take your time. You acquired these belongings over a lifetime, so why would you put yourself through the onerous task of dismantling your life in a week or a month? Commit to one big garbage bag per day. If you do two per day, take Sunday off.

(4) Out of sight, out of mind. You will be surprised how quickly you forget about items once they're gone. Anyone who has moved house and lived without their belongings for a period of time will have experienced this. Our stuff becomes part of our identity. Sure, everyone has their own treasures - a piece of artwork that won't take up too much space on a wall - but you may be surprised how quickly you forget about items once they're out of sight.

The emotional labor is often as challenging as the physical labor.

(5) Stop buying. Some countercultural advice this Black Friday - stop buying stuff that replaces the stuff you threw out. Perhaps it's that 2026 holiday sweater that looks so enticing online, even when we have a closet full of old sweaters crying out to be worn. We all love a bargain, and Black Friday and Cyber Monday tempt us to spend, spend, spend (analysts forecast spending nearing $30 billion for both "consumer holidays" this year). Don't replace the stuff you throw out.

Make spring cleaning an annual or semiannual event. As writer Evelyn Richards noted in this personal reflection in Country Living Magazine about downsizing from a three-bedroom house to a one-bedroom apartment: "Decluttering isn't just about tidying up your home; it's also about nurturing your mental well-being. When you clear out the excess and organize your space, you create a serene and stress-free environment."

It feels lighter to walk into a room where everything is in order, she writes. "This kind of order can significantly reduce anxiety and make it easier to relax. When your home is clutter-free, it's like a breath of fresh air, allowing you to focus on what truly matters. Moreover, the process of decluttering itself can be therapeutic. As you sort through items, you make decisions about what to keep and what to let go, which can be incredibly empowering."

I'm resisting buying yet another pair of sneakers this Black Friday because, like you, I have too much stuff. I sometimes wonder how much money I would have saved in my life had I stuck to a black cashmere turtleneck like Apple's late CEO Steve Jobs or a black leather jacket like Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang. You have accumulated a lifetime of memories - and, presumably, a few savvy investments in artwork and furniture - and passing those treasures on to loved ones should be a joy. Still, even the most discerning consumer ends up with clutter.

The ceramic bunny rabbit has got to go.

Related: This is the best Black Friday purchase I ever made

Check out The Moneyist's private Facebook group, where members help answer life's thorniest money issues. Post your questions, weigh in on the latest Moneyist columns or email The Moneyist at qfottrell@marketwatch.com.

More columns from Quentin Fottrell:

I hate that Jensen Huang is back at Nvidia, but I love what it's done for my 401(k). Am I a hypocrite?

I'm in my 70s and buying a new BMW X1. Should I put my only son on the title?

I've been married for 58 years. It's 'our' money, not 'his' and 'hers.' Why do so many couples keep their finances separate?

Xtool Announces Lifetime Free Software Updates for Select Automotive Diagnostic Scanners, Including Previously Purchased Devices

PR Newswire

SANTA ANA, Calif., Nov. 27, 2026

SANTA ANA, Calif., Nov. 27, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XTOOL, a provider of professional automotive diagnostic solutions, today announced a major upgrade to its software update policy. Effective November 27, 2026, Lifetime Free Software Updates will be available for select XTOOL automotive diagnostic scanners, extending this benefit to both new customers and all existing owners of eligible models.

Under the updated policy, customers purchasing eligible devices, as well as those who purchased them previously, will receive applicable software updates for the lifetime of their devices without paying annual software renewal fees. This change helps reduce long-term ownership costs and delivers greater value to professional automotive technicians, advanced DIY enthusiasts, and vehicle owners.

The policy upgrade reinforces XTOOL's commitment to long-term customer support, helping users keep their diagnostic tools up to date as vehicle technologies and repair requirements continue to evolve.

A Major Policy Upgrade: No More Annual Software Renewal Fees

As automotive technology continues to advance, regular software updates are essential to maintaining the diagnostic capabilities of automotive scan tools. To deliver greater long-term value, XTOOL is introducing Lifetime Free Software Updates for select 7-inch and 8-inch scan tool series.

Eligible models include:
D Series: D7, D7S, D7W, D7X, D7PRO, D7BT, D8, and D8BT (V3.0).
INPLUS Series: IP819, IP900, and IP900BT.
The updated policy covers both new and existing owners:

  • New Customers: Customers who purchase any of the eligible models listed above will receive Lifetime Free Software Updates, with no annual software renewal fees.
  • Existing Owners: Customers who previously purchased any of the eligible models will also receive Lifetime Free Software Updates. There is no need to purchase a new device or pay additional annual software renewal fees to receive this benefit.

One Device. Lifetime Software Updates. This policy upgrade is designed to lower the long-term cost of ownership while helping users keep their diagnostic tools current with evolving vehicle technologies and service requirements.

Supporting Existing Customers: Exclusive Customer Appreciation Benefits

XTOOL values the trust and continued support of its customers. By extending Lifetime Free Software Updates to all existing owners of eligible models, the company is ensuring that longtime customers can enjoy the same software update benefits as new buyers.

In addition to this policy upgrade, XTOOL is preparing exclusive customer appreciation benefits for existing customers who recently purchased software renewal services. Customers with active paid software renewal subscriptions can contact XTOOL Customer Support to learn more about eligibility and redemption details. To help verify their purchases, customers should provide their device serial number and a screenshot of their software subscription or renewal purchase confirmation.

Customer Support: support@xtoolonline.com

XTOOL remains committed to listening to customer feedback, continuously improving its products and services, and delivering lasting value to its global user community.

Black Friday and Cyber Monday Deals: Save Up to 26.8% on Select Diagnostic Tools

data.title: Pittman & Davis Celebrates Its 100th Anniversary With Free Shipping Offer and a New Centennial Collection of Holiday Gifts
data.description:
Pittman & Davis Celebrates Its 100th Anniversary With Free Shipping Offer and a New Centennial Collection of Holiday Gifts

The Iconic Texas Citrus Brand Celebrates 100 Years of Delivering Farm Fresh Quality and Gifts Worth Remembering

Pittman & Davis is celebrating 100 years of sharing the finest fruit and food gifts of the American Sunbelt. The milestone traces back to a single Texas citrus grove and a belief that has guided the company for a century: every gift has a story. To mark the occasion, Pittman & Davis is offering free shipping sitewide for a limited time and introducing a new Centennial Collection of holiday gifts.

The company's story began in 1926 in Harlingen, Texas, when Frank Davis Sr., a 14 year veteran of the mail order business, partnered with H. Pittman, a local grower whose citrus was winning prizes. Frank knew mail order. Pittman knew citrus. Their Rio Grande Valley fruit soon found its way to tables across the country, and the Rio Ruby™ Red grapefruit became the company's signature. Today, Pittman & Davis still sources its citrus from family farms in the Rio Grande Valley and Florida's Indian River region, and its collection has grown to include pears, apples, smoked meats, cheeses, and pastries from small kitchens across the Sunbelt.

To celebrate the milestone, Pittman & Davis is introducing its Centennial Collection, a new assortment of holiday gifts that bring a century of Sunbelt flavor to the table:

  • Pittman & Davis 100 Year Anniversary Gift Basket: Created for the centennial, this keepsake red basket with rope handles holds Rio Ruby™ Red grapefruit, navel oranges, honey sweet tangerines, King Comice pears, and a Fuji apple, alongside caramel pecan popcorn, chocolate chip cookies, premium pistachios, hot honey peanuts, and dark chocolate sea salt caramels. It is a gift a hundred years in the making.
  • Holiday Treats Gift Tower: Navel oranges, King Comice pears, dark chocolate sea salt caramels, foil wrapped milk chocolates, and deluxe mixed nuts, stacked in exclusive Holiday Ornament boxes finished with a red satin ribbon.
  • Memorable Holidays Gift Boxes: Navel oranges, King Comice pears, and Fuji apples paired with Castello Gouda, artisan crackers, chocolate chip cookies, and holiday candies in an exclusive Holiday Ornaments gift box. The Deluxe box adds chocolates, deluxe mixed nuts, and sea salt vanilla caramels.

For a limited time, Pittman & Davis is also offering free shipping sitewide with promo code 1NXPR02. The Centennial Collection is available now at pittmandavis.com/centennial-celebration/c/p100.

“Frank Davis and Howard Pittman started this company in Harlingen in 1926, shipping Rio Grande Valley citrus to families across the country, and a hundred years later we’re still doing it,” said Alex Brown, President of Pittman & Davis. “Not many companies make it to a hundred years, and I’m so grateful that we’re here to celebrate it. I want to thank our team, who work hard every season on behalf of our customers, and I want to thank our customers for ordering from us year after year.”

The celebration continues on Instagram, where Pittman & Davis will host anniversary giveaways through the end of the year. Customers are invited to follow @pittmandavis on Instagram and watch for chances to win as the company marks its 100th year.

About Pittman & Davis

Since 1926, Pittman & Davis has delivered extraordinary food gifts that reflect the culinary and agricultural heritage of the American Sunbelt, with a lasting commitment to farm fresh quality and personal service. Its roots are in the Rio Grande Valley citrus groves of Harlingen, Texas, home of its signature Rio Ruby™ Red grapefruit. Pittman & Davis is part of the Indrio Fields family of brands. Learn more at pittmandavis.com.

data.title: 12 days of sardines and Croc charms: Are Advent calendars getting out of control?
data.description:
By Aditi Shrikant

Luxury Advent calendars in particular - which can run hundreds of dollars - have seen a spike in sales. Here's why.

"When the economy is not in a great place or when people feel very squeezed or stressed cash-wise, they will buy a little treat for themselves," one expert said.

Are Advent calendars reaching their peak?

Traditionally, these gift sets have counted down the days until Christmas with goodies like tiny chocolates tucked inside numbered boxes, drawers or doors, which you open each corresponding day in December leading up to the holiday. But if you've been scrolling through your social-media feeds lately, it's clear that this year's Advent calendars are getting more extra and unusual than ever.

Want 12 days of tinned fish? For $150, Fishwife has you covered with its Advent calendar featuring smoked salmon and chocolate sardines. Or perhaps you're in the market for Hello Kitty-themed Croc charms. Pay $60 and the "25 Days of Jibbitz" Advent calendar is yours.

And shoppers are buying it. Beauty-themed Advent calendars alone generated $40.2 million during the 2025 holiday season - up 33% over 2024, according to data from Circana. And this year could be even more profitable, as luxury-beauty Advent-calendar sales were already up 17% in September and October compared to last year, Circana said.

But people are not necessarily purchasing these as gifts, notes Mackenzie Shand, an executive editor at RetailMeNot. Turns out, 75% of shoppers planning to buy viral products are doing so for themselves, according to data from RetailMeNot.

So at a time when many Americans are being squeezed by inflation and struggling to fill their gas tanks, why are mystery boxes of tiny treats that can cost upwards of $300 flying off shelves?

Thank TikTok.

The perfect social-media product

Advent calendars tap into the unboxing trend that has grown into a massive marketing tool on video platforms like YouTube and TikTok, where creators open boxes of new products and give immediate reactions and reviews, instilling their followers with FOMO. Advent calendar interest rose 24% from last year, according to Launchmetrics, a data analytics company that tracks how social media affects product sales, and influencer posts about Advent calendars are also up 118%.

And the appeal of Advent calendars also overlaps with the growing interest in "blind boxes," or when shoppers order a mystery-style package, usually at a discounted rate, that contains unknown items. Posts with the hashtag #blindbox had 37.1 billion views on TikTok as of Monday afternoon, while #adventcalendar and #adventcalendaropening had 24 billion and 1.1 billion views, respectively.

While stores like CVS and Walmart sell Advent calendars with small samples of makeup and beauty supplies for between $25 and $30, the gift sets that have ignited the most discussion on YouTube, TikTok and Instagram are the luxury ones running for hundreds of dollars.

Take the Bloomingdale's Advent calendar, which contains 25 skin-care, beauty and home products for $350. Or luxe fragrance brand Jo Malone London is selling a 12-day Advent calendar with cologne and soap samples for $250. Even Fenty, known for being more accessible to shoppers who want quality makeup at a lower price, was initially selling its 12-product Advent calendar with face, lip and eye makeup for $248; it's been marked down to $190. And then there are the even more high-end boxes from the likes of Dior and Acqua di Parma running $800 and $1,022, respectively - and Dior's is sold out.

Much of the discussion around these Advent-calendar unboxing videos swirls around whether the gift sets are worth their high prices.

The $150 SKIMS Advent calendar, for example, went viral for containing just 12 items, most of which were hair ties and bobby pins. Many customers were furious. "This has gotta be rage bait," said one posting under the name Emily Meyers on TikTok, in a sentiment shared by many in the comments. "This actually is the worst Advent calendar to ever exist in the history of ever existing."

SKIMS ended up issuing an apology, and offered refunds to all customers.

Or the 24-product YSL calendar, which clocks in at $400 and includes makeup, skin-care and other beauty products, was called out by TikTok creator Elle Moonz for featuring "lip balm that looks like kids' makeup."

That hasn't stopped it from selling out, though. And Moonz ultimately decided that, overall, the Advent calendar was "worth it."

Elizabeth Pancotti, vice president of policy at the Groundwork Collective, a progressive advocacy group, said that many Advent calendars are filled with items that brands would be giving away for free. "The unfortunate thing is that people save up and buy something they think is going to be nice for themselves, and it's a bunch of free samples put into a box," she said.

But Alison Bringe, the chief marketing officer at Launchmetrics, said Advent calendars can be an affordable way to sample a brand's goods. A 100 milliliter Jo Malone fragrance usually clocks in at $175 - but for just $75 more for the Advent calendar, you get 11 more products, even if they are smaller. Plus, unboxing a mystery item from a shop you usually can't afford is exciting.

"Even as shoppers become more selective, Advent calendars still feel like good value, offering weeks of small luxury moments that are often worth more than the price tag and, for many, an entry point into a brand they might not otherwise buy into," Bringe said.

The 'lipstick effect'

Advent calendars are also tapping into the "lipstick effect," or "treat yourself," trend, when people indulge in their desire for a little bit of luxury during a tough financial period, said Pancotti of the Groundwork Collective.

"When the economy is not in a great place or when people feel very squeezed or stressed cash-wise, they will buy a little treat for themselves," she said. During the 2008 recession, for example, cosmetics spending increased for women ages 18 to 40, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

For many Americans who have been tightening their budgets all year, this indulgence might seem earned, said Hal Hershfield, a psychologist and professor of behavioral decision-making at the University of California, Los Angeles.

"If someone is skipping a holiday trip or cutting back on dinners out this year, the calendar can feel like the affordable version of a splurge they'd normally make," he said.

Plus, the love for Advent calendars also embraces the ongoing nostalgia trend of adults buying products that were traditionally marketed toward children, said Shand from RetailMeNot, likening them to the wildly popular Squishmallow plush toys or Labubus.

"What was once primarily a countdown for children has become a way for consumers of all ages," she said. "Advent calendars tap into that same desire for discovery, excitement and a little self-indulgence, making them an appealing purchase for shoppers who want to treat themselves."
